title: The Serpent, the Fruit, and the Way Out of Eden
summary: A crafty serpent questions God's word, and the woman and the man eat from the forbidden tree. Their eyes are opened, they hide from God, and when he confronts them each shifts the blame. God pronounces judgment on the serpent, the woman, and the man, promises that the woman's seed will crush the serpent's head, clothes the couple with garments of skin, and sends them out of the garden, with cherubim guarding the way to the tree of life.
story: Chapter 2 ended with a man and a woman naked and unashamed in a garden full of good gifts, under one command. Chapter 3 tells how that world was lost. It is the hinge between creation and everything after it. From here on, the Bible's story is about a good world gone wrong and a God who will not let it go. Death, pain, hard labor, broken relationships, and distance from God all enter here, and they spread fast in the chapters that follow: a brother's murder in chapter 4, a line of deaths in chapter 5, and violence filling the earth in chapter 6. But grace enters too. God comes looking, he speaks a promise about the serpent's defeat, and he makes clothes for the people he is sending away. The rest of Scripture can be read as the long answer to the question God asks in verse 9, “Where are you?”
historical:
The chapter belongs to the same account as chapter 2 (the account of the heavens and the earth, 2:4-4:26), and like it, it speaks to a world full of stories about serpents, trees, and lost chances at life. In the eleventh tablet of the Babylonian Epic of Gilgamesh, the hero finally obtains a plant that restores youth, only to have a snake steal it while he bathes in a pool; the snake sheds its skin, and Gilgamesh weeps for his lost chance to escape death. In the myth of Adapa, known from a tablet found at el-Amarna in Egypt and dated to the fourteenth century BC, the wise man Adapa is summoned to heaven, where the god Anu offers him the bread and water of life; warned by the god Ea to refuse what he is offered, he declines and remains mortal. Both stories share with Genesis the themes of wisdom, food, and forfeited life, and both differ from it sharply: in Genesis the loss comes not from a trick or an accident but from disobedience, and God is not a rival guarding immortality from humans out of jealousy.

Serpents carried many meanings in the ancient world. In Egypt the cobra (the uraeus) rose from Pharaoh's crown as a sign of royal power and protection, while the great serpent Apophis was the enemy of the sun god, fought every night. Serpents could stand for wisdom, healing, fertility, or chaos, and in Canaan they appear on cult objects; at Timna in the Arabah, Beno Rothenberg found in 1969 a small copper snake with a gilded head in a shrine used by the Midianites, which recalls the bronze serpent of Numbers 21 that Hezekiah later destroyed (2 Kings 18:4). Genesis is careful about what it does with this image. The serpent is a creature, one of the beasts of the field that the LORD God had made, not a rival god, and it has no power except the power of speech.

Genesis itself does not name the serpent as Satan. Later Jewish writers began to connect the fall with a spiritual enemy. The Wisdom of Solomon (2:24, first century BC) says that death entered the world through the devil's envy. The Life of Adam and Eve, preserved in Greek as the Apocalypse of Moses, has the devil speak through the serpent, and 1 Enoch 69:6 names a fallen angel, Gadreel, as the one who led Eve astray. The New Testament makes the link openly when Revelation calls the devil “that ancient serpent” (Revelation 12:9, 20:2), and Jesus calls the devil a murderer from the beginning and the father of lies (John 8:44). The cherubim of verse 24 also belong to the ancient world. Assyrian palace gates were guarded by colossal winged figures with human heads and the bodies of bulls or lions, and Phoenician and Israelite ivories show winged sphinxes flanking thrones and sacred trees. Israel's own tabernacle and temple had cherubim over the ark and woven into the curtain that barred the way into the Most Holy Place.
cultural:
An ancient reader would have understood nakedness and clothing as matters of status and honor, not only of modesty. To be stripped was to be shamed, as prisoners and captives were (Isaiah 20:4), and to clothe someone was an act of care or investiture. So it matters that the couple's first act after eating is to cover themselves with fig leaves, the largest leaves in the land and ones that could be sewn into rough loincloths, and that God's last act before sending them out is to make them better garments. The word for those garments, kuttonet (tunic), is the word used for Joseph's special robe (Genesis 37:3) and for the tunics of Aaron's sons, and the verb clothe (lavash) is the one used when Moses clothes the priests at their ordination (Exodus 28:40-41, Leviticus 8:13). The detail links the gift of covering with the later clothing of God's servants.

The phrase in the breeze of the day (verse 8) is usually taken to mean the cool, windy part of the afternoon or evening. Jeffrey Niehaus (Vetus Testamentum, 1994) argued instead for ‘in the wind of the storm’, reading yom in light of an Akkadian word for storm, so that God comes in a thunderous theophany of judgment; most commentators have not followed him, but the proposal shows that the scene is more than a stroll. The sound (qol) the couple hear is the same word used for God's voice and for thunder.

The judgments speak to the core of each person's life in an agricultural world. For the woman, the pain touches bearing children, a real danger in a world where women often died in childbirth (as Rachel does in Genesis 35:16-19), and her closest relationship. For the man, the ground itself now resists him, producing thorns and thistles, and bread comes only through sweat. The same Hebrew word for painful toil (itsavon) is used for her childbearing and his farming, and it occurs only once more in the Bible, when Lamech names Noah in hope of relief from the toil of the cursed ground (5:29). To eat dust (verse 14) was an image of defeat and humiliation; conquered enemies lick the dust (Psalm 72:9, Micah 7:17), and ancient art shows vanquished kings bowing with faces to the ground. Isaiah's vision of the new creation keeps this one detail: the wolf and the lamb feed together, but dust remains the serpent's food (Isaiah 65:25).
literary:
The chapter is a finely built drama told mostly through dialogue. The serpent's first line is a question that twists God's word: God had given every tree but one, and the serpent asks whether he forbade them all. The woman corrects it but adds a detail of her own (or touch it), drops the generous ‘freely’ of 2:16, and softens the penalty from you will surely die to lest you die. The serpent then contradicts God flatly, using God's own emphatic construction with a negative (‘you will not surely die’), and offers a new picture of God as a jealous withholder. Verse 6 echoes the language of 2:9, now seen through desire: good for food, pleasing (ta'avah, craving) to the eyes, desirable (chamad, the verb of the tenth commandment's covet) for wisdom. The narration then speeds up into a chain of short verbs: she saw, took, ate, gave, and he ate. The man, the text says, was with her.

The promise that their eyes will be opened comes true with bitter irony, since what they see is their own nakedness. The verb eat occurs seventeen times in the chapter, and the key words of chapter 2 return reversed: the ground, the tree, the command, nakedness, and dust. Then the order of the story reverses. The sin moved from serpent to woman to man; God's questions move back from the man to the woman, and the serpent is never questioned; the judgments run forward again, from serpent to woman to man. Gordon Wenham and others describe the whole chapter as a mirrored pattern (a chiasm, or palistrophe) that puts God's questioning at the center. The judgments of verses 14 to 19 are set as poetry, and only the serpent and the ground are said to be cursed; the man and the woman are judged but not cursed.

God's own speech frames the end. Verse 22 breaks off in the middle of a sentence (‘lest he reach out his hand, and take also from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever’), a device called aposiopesis, and the action of verses 23 and 24 completes the thought. The chapter ends with a guarded road east, the direction of exile in Genesis: Cain settles east of Eden (4:16), and the builders of Babel travel from the east (11:2). The next chapter repeats this one's pattern closely: God asks Cain where his brother is, as he asked the man where he was; sin's desire for Cain and his rule over it (4:7) use the same words as the woman's desire and the man's rule (3:16); and Cain, like his parents, is driven out.

outline.t: They eat, and their eyes are opened
God seeks them, and they shift the blame
The serpent cursed and the promise of the woman's seed
Pain in childbirth, toil on the ground, return to dust
Eve named, the couple clothed and sent from the garden

doctrines.note: Sin begins not with a crime but with a question about whether God can be trusted, followed by the choice to decide good and evil for oneself. Its results are immediate: shame, fear, hiding, blame, and broken relationships with God, with one another, and with the ground. The church has read this chapter as the origin of the human condition, though Western and Eastern traditions, and Jewish readers, differ on how Adam's sin affects his descendants (see the interpretation note).

God said that in the day they ate they would surely die, and they did not drop dead that day. The same idiom is used when Solomon warns Shimei that on the day he leaves Jerusalem he will surely die (1 Kings 2:37); the sentence becomes certain that day, and is carried out later. Death as mortality and as separation from God began at once, and exile from the garden made it visible. The judgments are real, but only the serpent and the ground are cursed.

Verse 15 promises lasting conflict between the serpent's seed and the woman's, ending with the serpent's head crushed. It is the first hint in Scripture that God will defeat evil through a human descendant. Jewish Targums read it of a victory in the days of the King Messiah, and Christians since Irenaeus have read it as the first announcement of the gospel, fulfilled in Christ.

Before the couple leaves the garden, God has already begun to act for them. He seeks them out with a question, promises a victory over the serpent, lets the man name his wife mother of all the living in the face of death, and covers their shame with garments he makes himself. Grace appears in the same chapter as the fall.

The chapter ends with the first exile: humanity is driven out of God's presence, east of Eden, with the way back barred. The pattern of sin, judgment, and expulsion from the place of blessing recurs in Cain's wandering and above all in Israel's exile from the land, and the prophets speak of the return as a new Eden (Isaiah 51:3, Ezekiel 36:35).

words.note: Arum, translated crafty. It occurs eleven times, eight of them in Proverbs, where it is a virtue: the prudent person sees danger and hides (Proverbs 22:3) and overlooks an insult (12:16). In Job it describes the schemes of the crafty (Job 5:12). So the word itself names shrewdness that can be used well or badly, and the serpent uses it badly. It is a deliberate echo of arummim, naked, in 2:25: the couple were naked and unashamed; the serpent was shrewd. By the end of the scene they have gained a kind of knowing and lost their innocence.

Nachash, serpent, snake. It occurs about thirty times: the serpent here, Moses' staff turned to a snake (Exodus 4:3), the fiery serpents and the bronze serpent in the wilderness (Numbers 21:6-9), and Leviathan the fleeing serpent whom God will slay (Isaiah 27:1). The same consonants spell a verb for divination (Genesis 44:5) and sound like the word for bronze (nechoshet), a play Numbers 21:9 exploits. The serpent thus gathers associations with secret knowledge, danger, and the chaos God overcomes.

Zera, seed or offspring. Like the English word, it can mean one descendant or a whole line of them, and it occurs more than two hundred times in its sense of offspring. In verse 15 it begins a thread that runs through Genesis, as God promises seed to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (12:7, 22:17-18, 26:4, 28:14). Whether the woman's seed means humanity in general, the line of the faithful, or one particular descendant is debated. C. John Collins (Tyndale Bulletin, 1997) argued that when zera means a whole posterity it is often construed with plural pronouns or verbs, while a singular independent pronoun like the one here is used only when a single child is meant; others hold that the singular pronoun simply agrees with the singular noun and leaves the question open.

Shuf, to crush, bruise, strike. It occurs only four times: twice in verse 15 and in Job 9:17 and Psalm 139:11, where the text is uncertain. The same verb is used for both actions, the seed's blow to the serpent's head and the serpent's blow to the seed's heel, which is why the King James Version reads bruise twice and the Septuagint reads ‘watch for’ twice. English versions that use crush and strike (BSB, NIV) are bringing out the difference in the targets: a blow to the head is fatal, a bite to the heel is painful but not final.

Teshuqah, desire, used only three times in the Hebrew Bible: here, 4:7 (sin's desire for Cain), and Song of Songs 7:10, where the bride rejoices that her beloved's desire is for her. Some read verse 16 as the woman's longing for her husband, which he will exploit by ruling over her. Susan Foh (Westminster Theological Journal, 1975) argued from 4:7 that it is a desire to control him, met by domination in return, a reading reflected in the ESV's 2016 revision (‘contrary to your husband’). On either reading the verse describes a relationship bent by sin, not God's original design.

Itsavon, painful toil. It occurs only three times, all in Genesis: for the woman's pain in childbearing (verse 16), for the man's toil on the ground (verse 17), and when Lamech names Noah in the hope that he will bring comfort from the toil of the cursed ground (5:29). The related noun etsev, pain, also appears in verse 16. Using one word for both judgments shows that the man and the woman share the same sorrow, each in the sphere of their calling, and that fruitfulness and work, the blessings of 1:28, now come through pain.

Arar, to curse, to place under a ban or bind with misfortune. It occurs about sixty times, including the twelve curses of Deuteronomy 27:15-26 and the curses of Deuteronomy 28. It is the opposite of the blessing God spoke in chapter 1. Here it falls on the serpent and on the ground because of the man, and it will fall on Cain in 4:11 and Canaan in 9:25. The call of Abraham in chapter 12 answers this spreading curse with a fivefold promise of blessing and the words “and all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3).

Keruv, cherub. It occurs about ninety times, almost all of them in the descriptions of the tabernacle and temple (two golden cherubim over the ark, cherubim woven into the curtains, carved on the temple walls) and in Ezekiel's visions of the living creatures who bear God's throne (Ezekiel 10). God is called the one enthroned between the cherubim (1 Samuel 4:4). Their first appearance, as guards of the way to the tree of life, sets their role: they mark the boundary of God's holy presence, which sinners cannot cross on their own terms.

christ:
Christian readers since the second century have heard in verse 15 the first announcement of the gospel, which later tradition named the protoevangelium, the first gospel. Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho 100) set Eve, who conceived the serpent's word and brought forth disobedience and death, beside Mary, who received the angel's word in faith, and Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.21.1) read the woman's seed as Christ, born of a woman, who crushes the serpent's head. The New Testament does not quote the verse directly, but it echoes it. Paul tells the Roman church, “The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet” (Romans 16:20). Hebrews says Christ shared our humanity “so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil” (Hebrews 2:14), and John writes that the Son of God appeared “to destroy the works of the devil” (1 John 3:8). Paul's phrase “born of a woman” (Galatians 4:4) may also recall the promise. The picture of a wounded heel and a crushed head fits the cross, where the victory comes through suffering; that is a Christian reading of a promise whose original words leave the victor's identity open, and it should be taught as fulfillment rather than as the verse's only possible sense.

Paul's fullest reading of this chapter comes in Romans 5, where he sets Adam and Christ side by side: “sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin” (Romans 5:12), and “just as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). He says the same in brief: “For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22). Many readers have also noticed that the first Adam failed in a garden of plenty while Christ, tempted in the wilderness while hungry, answered the tempter with God's word (Matthew 4:1-11), and Hebrews says he “was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). Paul also sees creation's frustration here, a world “subjected to futility” in hope of freedom (Romans 8:20-21).

The Bible's final vision answers the end of this chapter point by point. The way to the tree of life, barred by cherubim, is opened: “Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life” (Revelation 22:14). The curse pronounced here is lifted: “No longer will there be any curse” (Revelation 22:3). And the God who came walking in the garden and found people hiding from him now dwells with them, and they see his face (Revelation 22:4).
interpretation:
Jewish tradition read this chapter as the story of the first sin but did not, on the whole, develop a doctrine of inherited guilt. Sirach 25:24 (early second century BC) traced the beginning of sin and death to a woman. Two Jewish apocalypses written after AD 70 set out opposite emphases: 4 Ezra 7:118 laments that Adam's fall was not his alone but also that of his descendants, while 2 Baruch 54:19 insists that Adam is responsible only for himself and each person has become his own Adam. The rabbis spoke instead of the evil inclination (yetzer hara) present in every person. They also noticed the details. Avot de-Rabbi Natan (chapter 1) says Adam made a fence around God's command by telling Eve not to touch the tree, and that the serpent pushed her against it to prove she would not die, a warning against adding to God's word. Genesis Rabbah 20:11 plays on Eve's name (chavvah) and the Aramaic word for serpent (chivya). The Palestinian Targums (Neofiti and Pseudo-Jonathan) paraphrase verse 15 as a struggle between the woman's children and the serpent, with a remedy for her children and peace in the end, in the days of the King Messiah.

The church fathers read the chapter as the first act of a drama Christ reverses. Justin Martyr and Irenaeus drew the parallels of Adam and Christ, Eve and Mary; Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.22.4) wrote that the knot of Eve's disobedience was loosed by Mary's obedience. Augustine made pride the root of the first sin (City of God 14.13) and, in the controversy with Pelagius (from 411), developed the doctrine of original sin, the inherited guilt and corruption of Adam's race, which the Western church confirmed and the Council of Trent restated in its fifth session (1546). Eastern Orthodox theology has generally spoken instead of ancestral sin, stressing inherited mortality and corruption rather than guilt, a distinction sharpened in John Romanides' The Ancestral Sin (1957). Jerome's Vulgate read ‘she will crush your head’ (ipsa) in verse 15, which shaped Western art of Mary treading on the serpent and is echoed in Pius IX's bull Ineffabilis Deus (1854) on the Immaculate Conception. Luther's lectures read verse 15 as the gospel preached to Adam, and Calvin's commentary (1554) read the seed as the human race led by Christ its head. Reformed theology later spoke of a covenant of works made with Adam (Westminster Confession 7.2, 1646), sometimes citing Hosea 6:7.

Modern readers have multiplied the lenses. Kant's Conjectural Beginning of Human History (1786) read the story as humanity's step from instinct to freedom, and Kierkegaard's The Concept of Anxiety (1844) explored the anxiety that precedes Adam's leap into sin. Paul Ricoeur (The Symbolism of Evil, 1960) called it the Adamic myth, which alone places evil's origin in a human act rather than in the gods or matter. James Barr (The Garden of Eden and the Hope of Immortality, 1992) argued that the story tells of a lost chance at immortality rather than a fall, and R. W. L. Moberly (Journal of Theological Studies, 1988) asked whether the serpent got it right. Milton's Paradise Lost (1667) gave English its fullest retelling.

In worship the chapter is the first lesson of the Festival of Nine Lessons and Carols, read at King's College, Cambridge, since 1919, and the Revised Common Lectionary pairs 2:15-17 and 3:1-7 with Christ's temptation on the First Sunday in Lent (Year A). On Ash Wednesday, ashes are imposed in many churches with the words of verse 19. The Easter Exsultet praises Adam's sin as a happy fault that won so great a Redeemer. In art, Masaccio's Expulsion in the Brancacci Chapel in Florence (about 1425), Jan van Eyck's Adam and Eve on the Ghent Altarpiece (1432), Albrecht Dürer's engraving (1504), and Michelangelo's Temptation and Expulsion on the Sistine ceiling have shaped how the West imagines the scene.
text:
Several differences between English Bibles in this chapter come from ancient versions or from translation choices.

Verse 15 is the most important. The Hebrew pronoun is masculine singular, hu, ‘he’ or ‘it’, agreeing with seed. The Septuagint translates with the masculine autos although its word for seed (sperma) is neuter, a choice some scholars take as an early personal reading, and it renders the verb as ‘watch for’ or ‘lie in wait for’ in both clauses. The Latin Vulgate reads ipsa, ‘she’, referring to the woman, which shaped Catholic devotion to Mary; modern Catholic translations such as the New American Bible follow the Hebrew. The King James Version's ‘bruise’ in both clauses reflects the single Hebrew verb, while many modern versions use crush and strike.

In verse 6 some translations omit ‘who was with her’ (the phrase is present in the Hebrew but was left untranslated in the RSV and some others), which affects how readers picture the man's part. In verse 8, ‘the cool of the day’ (KJV, ESV, NIV), ‘the breeze of the day’ (BSB), and ‘the evening breeze’ (NRSV) render ruach hayyom; see the cultural note for a different proposal. In verse 16 the ESV (2016) changed ‘your desire shall be for your husband’ to ‘your desire shall be contrary to your husband’, an interpretive rendering discussed under teshuqah. In verse 17 the Septuagint reads ‘in your works’ for ‘because of you’, apparently reading a similar Hebrew word. In verse 20 the Septuagint translates Eve's name as Zōē, ‘life’, making the wordplay plain. In verse 22 the sentence breaks off unfinished in Hebrew, and English versions mark it with a dash or ellipsis. In verse 24 the Septuagint adds that God settled the man opposite the garden of delight. The verse numbers are the same in Hebrew and English Bibles.

teach.big: Sin begins by doubting God's word and grasping at what he withholds, and it brings shame, blame, and death, but God comes seeking, promises victory over the serpent, and covers the people he sends out.

outline.t: Temptation works by distorting God's word, shrinking his generosity, and recasting him as a rival who withholds good.
Sin is a grasping for wisdom apart from God; it promises open eyes and delivers shame.
Sin drives people to hide from God and blame others, but God comes seeking with questions that invite confession.
God curses the serpent and promises a lasting war that ends with its head crushed by the woman's seed, the first word of hope.
The consequences reach every sphere of life, childbearing, marriage, work, and the body, and end in a return to dust.
Even in exile there is grace: a name of life, garments from God's hand, and a guarded way to the tree of life that waits to be reopened.

teach.pitfalls:
The most damaging misuse of this chapter has been to blame women. Preachers from the early church onward have treated Eve as the gateway of sin and women as more easily deceived, and verse 16 has been used to justify husbands ruling harshly. The text holds both the man and the woman responsible; the man was with her, and it is Adam whom Paul names as the one through whom sin entered the world (Romans 5:12). Verse 16 describes what sin does to marriage, not what God commands husbands to do, and preaching it as a mandate for domination turns a curse into a program.

Other misreadings are common. Some make the fruit an apple (a Latin pun on malum, evil and apple) or the sin a sexual one; the text says neither. Some treat the serpent as a harmless symbol, others speculate at length about its anatomy before the curse; better to say what Genesis says and let the New Testament name the enemy behind it. Some read the chapter as moral advice (resist temptation) and stop there, missing God's pursuit, promise, and provision. Others preach verse 15 as if the Hebrew obviously named Christ; it is better to show the promise open in Genesis and fulfilled in the gospel. Finally, avoid presenting the scientific debate over Adam's historicity as the whole point, or dismissing it; state the options fairly and keep the chapter's plain teaching at the center.
teach.pastoral: This chapter presses on shame and blame, and on pain that can seem to have no cause. People who carry shame will recognize the hiding and the fig leaves; teach that God's first word is a question that seeks, and that he himself covers what they cannot. Women who have suffered in childbirth, who have miscarried, or who cannot conceive should not hear the chapter as a verdict that their pain is personal punishment; it describes a broken world, not a sentence on each sufferer. Anyone living with a harsh or abusive spouse must never hear verse 16 as God's approval of domination. And people grieving a death will hear verse 19 with weight; pair it with the chapter's hope and with the Bible's ending, where death and curse are no more.

hard.q: Were Adam and Eve real people, and does it matter?
hard.a:
The objection is strongest from population genetics. Geneticists such as Dennis Venema (Adam and the Genome, with Scot McKnight, 2017) argue that human genetic diversity shows our ancestral population never dropped below several thousand individuals, which rules out all humans descending from a single couple within the time frame the traditional reading assumes. Combined with the evidence for human evolution and with the chapter's symbolic features (a talking serpent, trees of life and knowledge, the name Adam meaning simply human), many scholars conclude that Genesis 2 and 3 is not history at all. Peter Enns (The Evolution of Adam, 2012) argues that Paul's use of Adam reflects the assumptions of his time and need not bind modern readers. Jewish tradition, from the Mishnah onward, has generally read Adam as the first human but without the Western doctrine of inherited guilt, and many modern Jewish readers take the story as instruction rather than history.

Christians who share the same confession about sin and salvation answer in more than one way, as Four Views on the Historical Adam (edited by Matthew Barrett and Ardel Caneday, 2013) shows. The traditional view, held by most of the church through its history and defended by C. John Collins (Did Adam and Eve Really Exist?, 2011), takes Adam and Eve as real ancestors of the race whose sin affected all their descendants. A second group, including John Walton (The Lost World of Adam and Eve, 2015), William Lane Craig (In Quest of the Historical Adam, 2021), and S. Joshua Swamidass (The Genealogical Adam and Eve, 2019), accepts an ancient human population and holds that Adam and Eve were nonetheless real individuals, whether as archetypal representatives, as early ancestors of all humans, or as a couple from whom everyone living at the time of Christ descends genealogically. A third view, argued by Denis Lamoureux and Enns, reads the chapter as a story about every human being, told in ancient Near Eastern form.

Those who insist on a historical Adam point to Paul, who builds his argument in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15 on one man's disobedience and one man's obedience, and to Luke's genealogy, which traces Jesus back to Adam. Those who read the chapter differently argue that Paul's point about universal sin and grace stands without settling modern questions of human origins. What all these readers affirm is what the chapter plainly teaches: humanity was made good, turned from God by its own choice, and cannot undo the damage by itself.

hard.q: Did the serpent tell the truth? God said they would die that day, and they didn't.
hard.a:
The objection is old and sharp. God said, “in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die” (2:17); the serpent said they would not die and that their eyes would be opened and they would be like God. They did not die that day, Adam lived to 930 (5:5), their eyes were opened (verse 7), and God himself says the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil (verse 22). Some ancient Gnostic texts from Nag Hammadi, such as the Testimony of Truth, cast the serpent as a teacher of true knowledge and the Creator as a jealous lesser god. Kant read the story as humanity's necessary step from instinct into freedom, and Erich Fromm (You Shall Be as Gods, 1966) read it as emancipation from authority. Among biblical scholars, James Barr (1992) argued that the threatened death did not come and that the story is about lost immortality, not a fall, and R. W. L. Moberly (1988) framed the question by asking whether the serpent got it right.

The responses turn on the text's idioms and irony. The phrase in the day that followed by you will surely die (mot tamut) is used in 1 Kings 2:37 and 42, where Solomon warns Shimei that on the day he leaves Jerusalem he will surely die; Shimei is executed later, and the formula means the sentence becomes certain on that day. Many commentators, Gordon Wenham among them, therefore read the death sentence as passed and begun that day, with expulsion from the tree of life making mortality certain, and they note that in Israel's thought banishment from God's presence was itself a kind of death. Moberly himself concluded that the writer cannot have meant the serpent to be right and God wrong, and that the threatened death must be understood as more than physical death. On knowing good and evil, readers differ: some take it as moral autonomy, deciding for oneself what is good; some as comprehensive knowledge (good and evil as a pair meaning everything); some as the knowledge of mature rule that God meant to give in his time. On each view the serpent told a truth that deceived, which is what the woman says: “The serpent deceived me” (verse 13).

observe: Compare what God said in 2:16-17 with what the serpent says in 3:1 and 3:4-5, and with the woman's reply in 3:2-3. What is added, removed, or changed?
Who does God question, in what order, and who is not questioned? In what order are the judgments given?
What does God do for the man and woman in verses 20 to 24 besides sending them out?
interpret: What kind of wisdom or knowledge were the man and woman grasping for, and why was taking it a rejection of God?
In what sense did they die on the day they ate?
How does verse 15 point forward to Christ, and what does it leave open in its original setting?
apply: The serpent's first move is a question about what God really said and whether he can be trusted. Where do you hear that question most loudly in your own life?
The man blames the woman, and the woman blames the serpent. Why is shifting blame such an instinctive response, and what would it look like to answer God honestly?
Before sending the couple out, God makes them clothing. What does that act suggest about how God treats people even when he judges them?
